title: Edenrise C2 — M8: The Speed of Trust

scenes.script_line: Think about a person you really trust at work. When they say they'll do something, you believe them. You can speak openly with them. You don't waste time second-guessing their intentions. And when something goes wrong, you know you can have an honest conversation and move forward.
scenes.visual_direction: Someone you trust at work: two grounds workers who clearly rely on each other — a tool handed over before it is asked for, easy eye contact, no hesitation.

scenes.script_line: Now imagine the opposite. Information gets withheld. Promises are made but not kept. Mistakes get hidden. People start checking up on each other, protecting themselves and questioning motives. Everything slows down.
scenes.visual_direction: The opposite: work stalling. Someone quietly hiding a mistake, two people avoiding each other, a job half-done and left, a worker re-checking another's work behind their back.

scenes.script_line: This is one of the central ideas in Stephen M. R. Covey's The Speed of Trust: When trust goes up, speed goes up and cost goes down. When trust goes down, speed goes down and cost goes up.
scenes.visual_direction: The central idea as motion: a crew moving fast and smoothly through a job, contrasted with the same kind of work grinding slowly.
scenes.onscreen: Trust up → speed up, cost down.  Trust down → speed down, cost up.

scenes.script_line: Covey describes this as the difference between a Trust Dividend and a Trust Tax. In a high-trust environment, communication is faster. Decisions are easier. People collaborate more freely. Problems are raised earlier.
scenes.visual_direction: The dividend: a short decision made on the spot between two workers, a problem pointed out early and calmly, hands working together on one task.

scenes.script_line: But low-trust organisations pay a tax. More meetings. More checking. More misunderstandings. More delays. And more stress.
scenes.visual_direction: The tax: the same work weighed down — repeated checking, a job re-done, a worker waiting with nothing to do, visible fatigue at the end of the day.

scenes.script_line: Trust isn't simply a nice value to put on the wall. It has a practical and economic impact. And every one of us contributes to it. So how do we build more trust? Here are six behaviours we can start practising immediately.
scenes.visual_direction: Not a poster but a practice: a values card pinned in a shed, then hands actually doing the work. Every person on the crew contributes.

shots.text: a values card pinned on a shed wall, nobody reading it
shots.pexels: card pinned on shed wall

shots.text: hands actually doing the work instead, soil and tools
shots.pexels: hands working soil with tools

shots.text: wide of the whole crew at work, each person contributing
shots.pexels: whole crew at work each contributing

scenes.script_line: Number one: talk straight. Say what you mean. Be honest about problems. Have the conversations that need to be had. Talking straight doesn't mean being aggressive or insensitive. It means being clear, respectful and truthful. Instead of allowing frustration to build, say: "I think we may have a problem here. Can we talk about it?" A short, honest conversation today can prevent a much larger problem tomorrow.
scenes.visual_direction: Talk straight: two workers having the honest conversation calmly, face to face beside the work — open hands, steady eye contact, no aggression.

scenes.script_line: Number two: create clarity. A surprising amount of conflict comes from unclear expectations. One person thinks success means one thing. Another thinks it means something completely different. Before important work begins, get clear. What are we trying to achieve? Who is responsible for what? When does it need to happen? And what does a successful result look like? Clarity builds confidence. Ambiguity creates distrust.
scenes.visual_direction: Create clarity: a foreman and crew around a plan on a tailgate before the work starts — pointing at the drawing, marking out the ground, agreeing who does what.

scenes.script_line: Number three: keep commitments. Trust is built when our words and actions match. If you say you are going to do something, do everything you reasonably can to follow through. Sometimes circumstances change. The important thing is to communicate early. If you can no longer deliver what you promised, say: "Something has changed. Here's the situation, and here's what I propose we do." Trust does not require perfection. It requires integrity.
scenes.visual_direction: Keep commitments: a worker finishing the job they said they would, in the rain if needed; and telling a colleague early when something has changed.

scenes.script_line: Number four: practise accountability. When something goes wrong, low-trust cultures ask: Who can we blame? High-trust cultures ask: What happened? What can we learn? And how do we fix it? If you made the mistake, own it. Imagine someone simply saying: "That was my responsibility. I got it wrong. Here's what I'm doing to correct it." Taking responsibility doesn't weaken credibility. Very often, it strengthens it.
scenes.visual_direction: Accountability: a worker owning a mistake in front of the crew — hand on chest, calm face — then putting it right with their own hands.

scenes.script_line: Number five: listen first. Many trust problems begin with assumptions. We assume we know why someone behaved a certain way. We assume they don't care. We assume they had bad intentions. But assumptions are not facts. Instead, become curious. Ask: "Help me understand what happened." Listen before defending. Understand before judging. People are far more likely to trust us when they feel genuinely heard.

scenes.script_line: Number six: extend trust. Trust also has to be given. If capable people are constantly monitored and second-guessed, eventually they stop taking initiative. Strong leaders give people appropriate responsibility and allow them to own the result. That doesn't mean blind trust. It means what Covey describes as smart trust. Consider the situation. Consider the person's competence and character. Then give them enough trust to act. Responsibility grows when people are trusted with responsibility.

scenes.script_line: So here is a simple challenge. During the next week, pay attention to the trust you create around you. Ask yourself: Do I speak honestly? Do I make expectations clear? Do I keep my commitments? Do I take responsibility for my mistakes? Do I genuinely listen? And do I give trustworthy people the opportunity to take ownership?
scenes.visual_direction: The challenge: a worker alone at the end of a shift, thinking it over and writing the questions down in a small notebook.
scenes.onscreen: Your week: honest · clear · committed · accountable · listening · trusting

scenes.script_line: Trust is not created by one big event. It is created through hundreds of small moments. A promise kept. A difficult truth spoken respectfully. A mistake acknowledged. A person listened to. A responsibility entrusted.
scenes.visual_direction: Hundreds of small moments, shown as small moments: a hand shaking on a deal by the fence, a quiet word, a correction accepted, a key or tool passed over.

scenes.script_line: Over time, those moments create something extremely valuable. A team where people can move quickly because they don't have to protect themselves from one another. A team where communication becomes easier. Where accountability becomes normal. And where more energy can be spent doing great work. So if you want better communication, stronger teamwork and better performance, start with trust. Because when trust increases, almost everything else becomes easier.
